comment: Parking on bevacizumab alone is the smallest swing here: GOG-218 (pmid:22204724) gave HR 0.717 with no ITT OS gain. For an R0 patient whose ctDNA cleared to Not Detected, deep platinum response, that biology reads HR-deficient, and waiting it out underspends a curative-intent maintenance window. I would rather pre-position the HRD-gated PARP play than hold on the lowest-magnitude axis.

I am with the critic that niraparib is the no-wait drug, but burying olaparib+bevacizumab at rank 3 on RoB purity undersells the biggest effect on the board: the PAOLA-1 HRD-positive subgroup hit HR 0.33 with 5-year OS 66% vs 48% (pmid:31851799). She already gets bevacizumab, so the add-on is the cleanest path to that magnitude if HRD reads positive. Calling a pre-specified subgroup non-confirmatory is fair on paper but costs her the largest available upside.

Niraparib is a defensible rank 1, but writing the on-study GEN-1/IMNN-001 program out of the list entirely ignores preferences.json::prefers_trials=true and the fact she is already enrolled. OVATION-2 read median OS 40.5 vs 29.4 months (nct:NCT03393884) and OVATION-3 (nct:NCT06915025) lets her layer PARP onto the IL-12 axis. Guideline-only ranking is clean, but it drops a high-upside trial-continuity path she has explicitly asked for.

I am targeting the advocate rank-2 letrozole rather than rank-1 bevacizumab because that is where the veto-avoidance logic overreaches: it puts a tier-4 cohort (pmid:29157627, ROBINS-I serious, 60% vs 38.5% at 24 months, PR-negative) above niraparib. At efficacy_toxicity_weight 0.7 she is efficacy-leaning, and spending a top slot on a low-magnitude endocrine option to dodge a manageable, dose-individualized cytopenia risk inverts her own stated trade-off.

Ranking olaparib plus bevacizumab first puts a PARP inhibitor on top of ongoing anti-VEGF therapy in a woman the preferences file flags for high VTE risk and a prior IVC filter, and the risktaker names that bleeding hazard without a mitigation for it. PAOLA-1 (pmid:31851799) also adds grade 3-4 anemia of 17% versus under 1% on bevacizumab alone, so the same pick brushes her severe-myelosuppression veto from a second direction. I veto this stack as a rank-1 unless and until the HRD score returns positive and a concrete bleeding/VTE and CBC monitoring plan is on the table.

The critic ranks niraparib first at confidence high, but PRIMA (pmid:31562799) carries grade 3+ anemia of 31% and thrombocytopenia of 28.7% in the primary analysis, which sits directly on her stated severe-myelosuppression veto. The 3.5-year update pushing cumulative grade 3+ thrombocytopenia to 39.7% is not a footnote for a 70-79 patient on long maintenance. I dissent on the confidence, not the drug: the individualized weight-and-platelet starting dose has to be named as the prerequisite mitigation before this earns a high-confidence rank-1.

I agree the NCCN category 1 footing for olaparib plus bevacizumab is real once HRD reads positive, and the concensusite is right to keep it conditional. My qualifier is that the guideline endorsement was written for the PAOLA-1 population, not specifically for a patient carrying her bleeding and VTE history with a prior IVC filter, and pmid:31851799 adds grade 3-4 hypertension of 19% and anemia of 17% on top of the bevacizumab she already receives. Endorse the conditional ranking, but make the bleeding/VTE workup an explicit gate alongside the HRD result, not an afterthought.

This is the right rank-1 while the assay is out. Continuing the bevacizumab she already tolerates clears both toxicity vetoes, and GOG-218 (pmid:22204724) gives the regimen more than a decade of safety follow-up in her exact 1L indication with hypertension at grade 2+ around 22.9% as the dominant and well-managed event. The one thing I would keep on the chart, as the advocate already notes, is that her bleeding and thrombotic risk is accepted rather than absent, so the IVC-filter history stays on the active monitoring list.

Ranking GEN-1 third puts an unpublished result onto a treatment list. The OVATION 2 numbers come from SITC 2024 and ASCO 2025 toplines with no PMID and no peer-reviewed primary paper, so I cannot read its bias profile at all, and the BRCAm/HRD subgroup you lean on is n=34 with an OS HR confidence interval of 0.11-1.70 that crosses 1. That is too weak to cite as a basis for treatment, which is exactly what the veto guards against.

We agree letrozole stays low on tier, and your rank-3 rationale already names the problem: a single non-randomized cohort, ROBINS-I:Serious, n=80, 60% vs 38.5% recurrence-free at 24 months (pmid:29157627). My one ask is narrow. Keep the ROBINS-I:Serious label and the non-randomized design visible in any rendered table, so nobody downstream reads the 60% figure as if it came from an RCT.

I land in the same place on niraparib, but your rank-1 leans on the NCCN v3.2025 category 2A listing, and 2A is expert consensus rather than the evidence that actually carries this pick. The real warrant is PRIMA (pmid:31562799), a low-RoB double-blind phase 3 that hit its registered ITT PFS endpoint at HR 0.62 (0.50-0.76). Cite the trial first, since a consensus tier can shift between guideline versions while the RCT result does not.

Putting letrozole at rank 2 reads it almost entirely off preference_fit (oral, no marrow toxicity), and on that axis you are right that it clears her vetoes. On evidence it is the weakest pick you list: pmid:29157627 is a non-randomized cohort, ROBINS-I:Serious, n=80, and her PR-negativity tempers the expected magnitude further. Rank it for preference if you want, but the evidence gap belongs next to the rank, not tucked into the concerns where a reader can miss it.

Ranking the GEN-1/IMNN-001 program at 3 puts a conference-topline signal (nct:NCT06915025) ahead of NCCN Ovarian v3.2025-endorsed maintenance with no peer-reviewed primary paper and a BRCAm/HRD subgroup CI of 0.11-1.70 on 34 patients. No consensus guideline lists IL-12 immunogene therapy in this setting, so it belongs in her on-study context, not on the recommendation list. The trial-continuity argument is fair, but it does not move an investigational regimen to a guideline-fit pick.

Continuing the bevacizumab she already tolerates is the cleanest guideline-aligned hold while the HRD assay is out: NCCN Ovarian v3.2025 keeps it a category 2A 1L maintenance option on GOG-218 and ICON7 (pmid:22204724). The PFS-only caveat and the high-risk-subgroup survival signal are stated accurately, and neither touches her myelosuppression or neuropathy veto. This is exactly where the consensus would park her until the genomic-instability score returns.

Dropping bevacizumab to rank 4 mainly because GOG-218 and ICON7 are PFS-only (pmid:22204724) discounts a regimen NCCN Ovarian v3.2025 still carries at category 2A; that 2A is the panel's calibration of the same PFS data the critic is reading, not an oversight about missing OS. For a patient already on the agent with both her vetoes clear, the consensus weights it higher than fourth. The RoB read is sound, but guideline-fit and OS-purism pull in opposite directions here.

Letrozole at rank 2 reads on her preferences, and NCCN Ovarian v3.2025 does list aromatase inhibitors among hormone-therapy options for ER-positive disease, so it is not off-guideline outright. But the maintenance evidence is a non-randomized cohort (pmid:29157627), which the guideline never elevates to frontline maintenance alongside the category 1/2A PARP and bevacizumab data. I would hold it as a later-line or low-toxicity option rather than second on the list, and her PR-negativity tempers the magnitude further.

Ranking the olaparib add-on first puts a second anemia source (grade 3+ ~17%) and hypertension (~19%) per PAOLA-1 on top of bevacizumab, which compounds exactly the thrombotic/bleeding caution her preferences flag given her high VTE history and prior IVC filter. For a patient weighted 0.7 toward efficacy but still naming a severe-myelosuppression veto, I cannot put this on top while the HRD score it depends on is still pending. Niraparib does not wait on that assay, so leading with the gated combination spends her bleeding-risk budget on a benefit she may not be eligible for.

This is the pick that asks nothing new of her: continuing bevacizumab touches neither the neuropathy veto nor the severe-myelosuppression veto, and the GOG-218/ICON7 base (pmid:22204724) covers her exact 1L setting. The bleeding and VTE caution in her preferences is real, but it is a risk already built into the regimen she tolerates rather than a fresh one. Holding this axis steady while the rank-1 HRD assay returns is the lowest-regret move for her, and I read it the same way.

The evidence case for niraparib at rank 1 is clean and I do not dispute it, but PRIMA's grade 3+ anemia (31%) and thrombocytopenia (28.7%) per pmid:31562799 land right on her stated severe-myelosuppression veto. It is oral, which her modality preference rewards, so I will carry it for her only with the weight-and-platelet individualized starting dose named up front as the prerequisite, not as a footnote. Without that mitigation written into the pick, ranking the most cytopenia-prone option first reads past the toxicity she specifically asked us to avoid.

Guideline fit and the all-comers PRIMA benefit (pmid:31562799) make niraparib a defensible lead, and the oral schedule suits her preference for low-burden therapy. My one reservation on her behalf is that the dominant grade 3+ events are the cytopenias her severe-myelosuppression veto names, and her age band 70-79 sits at the older end of the enrolled population. The individualized starting dose is the only thing that keeps this aligned with her preferences, so it has to travel with the recommendation rather than soften it after the fact.
